strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive design: The paper builds upon the observation that models often exploit brittle high-frequency visual shortcuts that cause overconfidence under distribution shift. The insight that DCT low-pass filtering improves shift calibration but hurts in-distribution (ID) calibration due to underconfidence is well identified and directly targeted.

Principled optimization formulation: Formulating ID calibration as a hard first-order constraint via one-sided geometric projection neatly resolves the trade-off without introducing sensitive scalar balancing hyper-parameters.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span synthetic corruption benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world shift benchmarks (WILDS: Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), and semantic shift (Office-Home). The proposed FGR consistently yields superior or competitive ECE/ACE/CECE metrics while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Extensive ablations and analyses: The manuscript includes comparisons against symmetric multi-task gradient techniques (PCGrad, CAGrad), evaluations across modern vision transformers (ViT, Swin, DeiT), compatibility checks with post-hoc temperature scaling, runtime complexity analysis, and gradient conflict dynamics throughout training.
weaknesses: Algorithmic components are largely adaptations of existing tools: DCT-based frequency filtering is standard in frequency-domain robustness literature, and orthogonal gradient projection is directly adopted from multi-task gradient surgery (e.g., PCGrad/PAG), albeit used here in an asymmetric one-sided manner.

Sensitivity to training schedule: For training from scratch, FGR relies on a delayed activation (epoch 200) after a warm-up phase. As shown in Figure 7, starting too early hurts ID accuracy while starting too late dampens calibration benefits, adding training schedule complexity.

Theoretical depth is modest: Proposition 4.1 merely restates standard Euclidean projection onto a halfspace and a first-order Taylor expansion, which provides a sanity check for the gradient projection formula rather than substantial new theoretical insight.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual framework: The observation that low-pass filtering eliminates high-frequency shortcut features to improve out-of-distribution robustness—while simultaneously risking underconfidence and fine-grained discrimination loss in-distribution—provides a compelling foundation for the proposed approach.

Principled asymmetric gradient rectification: Formulating ID calibration as a hard first-order constraint via one-sided geometric projection neatly resolves the trade-off between out-of-distribution robustness and in-distribution calibration, avoiding the need for manual hyperparameter search over loss-balancing scalar weights.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper tests across diverse shift benchmarks, including synthetic corruptions (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world distribution shifts (WILDS: Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), and semantic visual shifts (Office-Home), as well as across multiple architectures (CNNs and Vision Transformers).

Thorough ablations and analysis: The manuscript includes comparison against standard multi-objective gradient projection baselines (PCGrad, CAGrad) and weighted-sum losses, gradient conflict dynamics across training epochs, compatibility with multiple differentiable calibration losses (Soft-AvUC, MMCE, Brier Score), and an efficient two-stage fine-tuning formulation.
weaknesses: Limitations of the theoretical guarantee under stochastic optimization: Proposition 4.1 assumes deterministic gradients and sufficiently small step sizes. In practice, $g_{\text{calib}}$ and $g_{\text{main}}$ are noisy stochastic estimates computed over mini-batches, where gradient noise and loss curvature can lead to constraint violation; the manuscript would benefit from explicitly discussing how mini-batch stochasticity affects the theoretical non-increase guarantee.

Sensitivity to training schedule and warm-up epoch: When training from scratch, FGR relies on delaying the activation of filtering and rectification until epoch 200 (out of 350 epochs on CIFAR) to ensure initial convergence of discriminative boundaries. This introduces a schedule hyperparameter ($E_{\text{start}}$) that may require tuning across different architectures and dataset schedules.

Inconsistent gains across transformer architectures: In Table 5, for ViT-Small on CIFAR-10-C and Camelyon17-OOD, Dual Focal Loss (DFL) alone achieves a lower ECE than FGR (2.62% vs. 2.80% on CIFAR-10-C; 9.15% vs. 10.14% on Camelyon17-OOD). A brief discussion clarifying why the filtering/projection behaves slightly differently on standard patch-based ViT compared to Swin/DeiT would improve transparency.

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing the trade-off between out-of-distribution robustness and in-distribution calibration, properly identifying that low-pass filtering can cause underconfidence on clean data.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse distribution shifts, including synthetic corruptions (CIFAR-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world domain shifts (WILDS: Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), and semantic domain shifts (Office-Home).
Thorough ablation and comparative studies demonstrating the advantage of asymmetric gradient projection over symmetric multi-task methods (PCGrad, CAGrad) and simple weighted scalarization.
Good architectural generality demonstrated across both convolutional backbones (ResNet, DenseNet, WideResNet) and modern vision transformer backbones (ViT, Swin, DeiT).

Detailed practical analysis, including training overhead measurements, a computationally efficient two-stage fine-tuning alternative, and compatibility with post-hoc calibration methods like Temperature Scaling.
weaknesses: Moderate algorithmic novelty: the framework primarily combines known tools—namely DCT-based frequency filtering (widely used in robustness literature) and first-order gradient projection / surgery (adapted from multi-task learning into a one-sided half-space projection).

Reliance on multiple hyperparameters that require dataset- and architecture-specific tuning, particularly the focal loss focusing parameter gamma (which varies from 1.2 to 5.5 across architectures in Tables 9 and 10), filtering ratio rho, and start epoch.

The theoretical guarantee (Proposition 4.1) assumes true population gradients and infinitesimal step sizes, whereas in practice the ID calibration gradient is computed on small, noisy mini-batches of soft-binned ECE, which can introduce variance into the constraint boundary.
Performance improvements on more complex semantic shifts (such as Office-Home) and certain WILDS benchmarks (such as FMoW) are modest compared to existing calibration baselines like DFL or BSCE-GRA.
